General structure

In Sukuk al-Ijara, the holders are paid from the rent on a real asset, not from interest on a loan.

This explainer describes the general structure of Sukuk al-Ijara. It is not a HAYKALAH transaction, and the terms of each issue vary.

Sukuk al-Ijara are lease-based Sukuk. A special purpose vehicle holds a leased asset on behalf of the Sukuk holders, and the rent paid by the lessee funds the periodic distributions. Each issue rests on Ijara, a Shariah-compliant lease in which the owner of an asset lets another party use it for an agreed term in return for an agreed rent. This explainer follows a typical issue from the asset to maturity.

Step by step

Step 1 of 6

General structure

The originator chooses an asset that can be leased.

The issue starts with an asset that earns, or can earn, rent, such as a building or equipment. Its title and documents have to be in order, because the Sukuk rest on it.

  • Originator to The asset Owns the asset

All steps

  1. 01The originator chooses an asset that can be leased.

    The issue starts with an asset that earns, or can earn, rent, such as a building or equipment. Its title and documents have to be in order, because the Sukuk rest on it.

    • Originator to The asset Owns the asset

  2. 02An SPV is set up, and the structure is approved.

    A special purpose vehicle is set up to hold the asset on behalf of the Sukuk holders, usually acting as their trustee. A Shariah board reviews and approves the contracts, the asset and the documents before the issue.

    • Shariah board to SPV, issuer and trustee Review and approval before the issue

  3. 03The holders pay for the Sukuk, and the asset moves to the SPV.

    Investors buy the Sukuk through an appropriately licensed institution, because offering Sukuk is a regulated activity. The SPV uses the proceeds to buy the asset from the originator.

    • Licensed institution to Sukuk holders Offers the Sukuk (regulated activity)
    • Sukuk holders to SPV, issuer and trustee Issue proceeds
    • SPV, issuer and trustee to Originator Purchase price for the asset
    • Originator to SPV, issuer and trustee The asset

  4. 04The SPV leases the asset under an Ijara.

    The SPV leases the asset, often back to the originator, for an agreed term and rent. As lessor, the SPV keeps the responsibilities of ownership that the contract and the applicable Shariah standards assign to it.

    • SPV, issuer and trustee to Originator Ijara: use of the asset for an agreed term

  5. 05The rent funds the distributions.

    The lessee pays rent on the agreed dates, and the SPV passes it to the Sukuk holders as periodic distributions. Their return comes from the rent, not from interest on a loan.

    • Originator to SPV, issuer and trustee Rent
    • SPV, issuer and trustee to Sukuk holders Periodic distributions

  6. 06At maturity, the originator buys the asset back.

    At the end of the term, the originator usually buys the asset back under a separate promise given at the start. The SPV pays the price to the Sukuk holders, and the Sukuk end.

    • Originator to SPV, issuer and trustee Repurchase price, under a separate promise
    • SPV, issuer and trustee to Originator The asset
    • SPV, issuer and trustee to Sukuk holders Repurchase proceeds at maturity

The parties

Originator
Owns the asset and raises the funding
The asset
An asset that can be leased, such as a building or equipment
SPV, issuer and trustee
Holds the asset on behalf of the Sukuk holders
Shariah board
Reviews and approves the contracts, the asset and the documents
Licensed institution
Offers the Sukuk to investors, a regulated activity
Sukuk holders
Own the certificates and receive distributions from the rent

Who it suits

  • Owners of assets that earn rent, such as buildings with tenants, that want funding while keeping the use of the asset.

  • Public bodies and companies with assets that can be leased.

  • Banks and financial institutions structuring Sukuk for their clients’ assets, for approval by their own Shariah board.

Risks and conditions

  • A real asset is needed. The structure works only with an asset that can be leased, with its title and documents in order.

  • Ownership comes with responsibilities. The contract allocates the duties of ownership between lessor and lessee, within the limits that the applicable Shariah standards set.

  • The distributions depend on the rent. The holders rely on the lessee paying the rent on time.

  • The repurchase depends on the originator. At maturity, the holders rely on the originator keeping its promise to buy the asset back. How the repurchase price is set is reviewed by the Shariah board.

  • Approvals and regulation. No structure is final until a Shariah board approves it, and offering Sukuk to investors is a regulated activity, executed through appropriately licensed partners.

  • No guarantee of financing, returns or outcomes.

How HAYKALAH uses it

Ijara is one of the contracts FINA., HAYKALAH’s financial structuring practice, builds Sukuk on. Before any structure is chosen, FINA. tests an asset’s cash flows against bands such as occupancy and debt-service cover. In 2025 HAYKALAH prepared three income-producing assets in Riyadh for Sukuk and tokenization (early stage). In the stadium precinct framework it proposed in 2026, the completed stadium moves to an Ijara or a Wakala-Ijara; that framework is a proposal with no mandate. HAYKALAH does not issue, offer or deal in securities.

All figures indicative. Proposals are not mandates. Clients are not named until they consent.
